newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Kabila says he knows where refugees are.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Kabila says he knows where refugees are.

text.p: Zaire's rebel leader Laurent Kabila told U.N. and other officials on Sunday he knew the whereabouts of thousands of Rwandan refugees who fled from camps in eastern Zaire, rebel officials said.
But as Kabila's meeting with the officials continued, it was not immediately known whether he would permit relief supplies to be taken to the refugees.
Meanwhile, a group of 33 Hutu refugees who fled their camp when it was attacked last week were airlifted to Kigali in the first direct flight of refugees from Zaire to Rwanda.
U.N. officials said the 33 refugees who fled Kasese camp, about 35 km (20 miles) south of Kisangani, flew home from a two- and-a-half year exile aboard a special flight.
"You certainly cannot say an airlift has started," one official said. "This is just one flight, but nevertheless a start."
Kabila agreed to a joint meeting with United Nations, European Union and aid officials after separate talks with individual representatives on Saturday.
He was accompanied by his foreign policy strategist, Dizima Karaha, legal affairs commissioner Mwenze Kongoro and other rebel leaders.
The rebel officials told Reuters that Kabila was able to tell the meeting where the refugees had gone.
Earlier on Sunday, rebel troops again blocked aid workers and journalists from travelling from Kisangani to areas where the refugees were believed to have fled, aid officials said.
Officials, including U.N. regional representative Piers Gerety and European Union delegate Aldo Ajello, had pressed for talks with Kabila to try to break the deadlock over access.
Karaha said: "This joint meeting was necessary for us to clear up a number of things, and enabled us to get the joint views of the aid agencies."
The fate of over 50,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees who fled camps after attacks by villagers and rebel soldiers remained unclear.
"We have very little hard information," said Paul Stromberg, spokesman for the United Nations refugee agency UNHCR.
He said aid officials had pressed to meet Kabila, who arrived in Kisangani on Saturday night, to convince him of the need to get help to the refugees quickly.
"Even if we find them, the first question we have for Mr Kabila is what kind of assistance can we give them?" he said before Sunday's meeting.
Planes flying over dense forest south of Kisangani found no sign of refugees, although about 50 were ferried north across the Zaire River by villagers in dugout canoes on Saturday.
Stromberg said about 100 others had been sighted at Ubundu, some 125 km (80 miles) south of Kisangani, but he doubted they would have been part of any group that fled last week.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan has described rebel treatment of the refugees as "slow extermination".

Some refugees played a prominent role in the 1994 slaughter of an estimated 800,000 minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda, and Kabila told Reuters last week that criminals among them had transported their lawlessness to Zaire.
Refugees among those who crossed the river on Saturday could not give a clear picture of what happened to make them flee.
One man, clutching a Bible as he sat in the prow of a canoe, said soldiers had surrounded the camp on Tuesday but local Zaireans armed with machetes and axes had led a series of raids.
"There was a lot of shooting, but I didn't see where from or where at," he said. "We just ran away as fast as we could."
The 50,000-plus refugees at Kasese, about 35 km (22 miles) south of Kisangani, were among the last of over a million Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 to escape reprisal for the genocide.

Most returned in a huge wave of repatriation sparked by Kabila's sweeping rebel advance through eastern Zaire. This group instead marched nearly 500 kms (300 miles) west through dense jungle before being overwhelmed by hunger, exhaustion and illness just south of Kisangani.
It was there that the rebel army overtook them.
An outbreak of cholera was cited by rebels as the reason for delaying the start of a planned U.N. airlift of the refugees.
Rebel authorities have blamed local hostility to the refugees on envy sparked by the sight of tons of food and other aid being given to them by aid organisations.
Local Zaireans have looted U.N. warehouses and a train carrying supplies to the camps, but some of them said they had been urged on by rebel soldiers.
